data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A decentralized network of small, independently operated services is more resilient to correlated failure than a large service with high redundancy because organic heterogeneity prevents the 'synchronization cascades' inherent in standardized redundancy.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The failure trigger is universal to the protocol or underlying hardware (e.g., a CPU flaw or a fundamental TCP/IP bug), rendering implementation diversity irrelevant (SRC_008).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The decentralized network converges on a single dominant software provider (e.g., all small services use the same open-source framework), recreating the homogeneity of a centralized service (SRC_005).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The 'Diversity Threshold' (SCR_003): By utilizing diverse implementation stacks, operating systems, and configuration patterns, the decentralized network ensures that a single software bug or configuration error (the 'latent common cause') cannot affect a critical mass of the network. In contrast, a large service's internal redundancy typically relies on homogeneous clones, where a single 'poison pill' request or a global timeout setting (SCR_002) triggers a simultaneous failure across all redundant nodes.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
